title: Meghalaya grows bridges from living tree roots
body: In Meghalaya's Khasi and Jaintia Hills, builders guide the hanging roots of rubber fig trees across streams. The roots thicken and can fuse where they touch. The Meghalaya Biodiversity Board says a firm bridge often takes 15 to 25 years to grow.
takeaway: The tree keeps growing after people start using the bridge, so its roots can strengthen the crossing over time.
source: Meghalaya Biodiversity Board and Ludwig et al., Scientific Reports (2019)
visual: a footbridge of intertwined living roots spanning a rocky stream beneath a rubber fig tree in Meghalaya
